checks.claim: Every element after hydrogen has two or more protons; the strong force is the strongest of the four fundamental forces
checks.note: Strength table: strong 0.1-1, electromagnetic 1/137, weak 1e-5, gravity 6e-39. Two or more protons after hydrogen follows from atomic number 2 upward.

checks.claim: Key: the strong force reaches only the particles right beside it
checks.note: Grokipedia: effective only to about 2-3 fm, then falls exponentially; saturation 'limits each nucleon's interactions to nearest neighbors'.

checks.claim: Wrong: reaches every particle in the atom, electrons too
checks.note: Truly wrong: leptons, electrons included, 'do not participate in the strong nuclear force' (no colour charge).

checks.claim: Wrong: reaches the nuclei of the atoms around it
checks.note: Truly wrong: negligible beyond about 2.5 fm, while neighbouring nuclei are about 10^-10 m away.

checks.claim: Wrong: reaches across space as far as gravity
checks.note: Truly wrong: strong range about 10^-15 m; gravity and electromagnetism have infinite range.

checks.claim: Context: strong force about a hundred times the electric push between two protons that close; acts on protons and neutrons alike
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'approximately 100 times that of the electromagnetic force between two protons'; nearly identical for pp, nn and pn pairs.

checks.claim: Context: fades to almost nothing beyond about 2.5 fm, two and a half trillionths of a millimetre
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'rapidly decreases to insignificance at distances beyond about 2.5 fm'. 2.5 fm = 2.5e-15 m = 2.5e-12 mm.

checks.claim: Context: because of its short reach the strong force 'never reaches the electrons'
checks.note: Minor, but a physicist would object: range is not why electrons escape it. Electrons do not feel the strong force at all, at any distance, and inner electrons spend part of their time inside the nucleus. The 'so ... never reaches the electrons' line teaches the wrong reason. Fix: '... so each particle grips only its nearest neighbours and never reaches the next atom; electrons do not feel it at all.'

checks.claim: Context: a big nucleus such as uranium's is fragile because every proton pushes on every other but grips only its neighbours
checks.note: Wikipedia: the Coulomb force between protons 'has a much greater range' than the nuclear force. This is the standard liquid-drop reason.

checks.claim: Between two protons gravity is about 10^36 (a trillion trillion trillion) times weaker than the electric force; gravity is by far the weakest
checks.note: Grokipedia: gravity is 'approximately 10^-36 times weaker than the electromagnetic interaction' for two protons. A trillion cubed is 10^36.

checks.claim: Gravity holds the Moon round Earth and Earth round the Sun
Key: mass only attracts, but plus and minus charges cancel
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'gravity always attracts and never repels'; astronomical bodies 'tend toward a near-neutral net electric charge'.

checks.claim: Wrong: the electric force fades with distance far faster than gravity
checks.note: Truly wrong: both go as 1/r^2; 'Electromagnetism has an infinite range, as gravity does'.

checks.claim: Wrong: the electric force cannot travel across empty space
checks.note: Truly wrong: electromagnetism has infinite range, carried by the massless photon.

checks.claim: Wrong: the Moon and Earth hold no charged particles at all
checks.note: Truly wrong: they are full of protons and electrons; only their net charge is near zero.

checks.claim: Context: the strong force and the weak force (behind some radioactive decay) reach no farther than a nucleus
checks.note: Weak range about 10^-18 m, mediates beta decay; strong range about 10^-15 m.

checks.claim: Hahn and Strassmann fired (slow) neutrons at uranium in Berlin late in 1938 and kept finding barium
checks.note: Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry, Berlin; runs culminating around 17 December 1938.

checks.claim: Hahn wrote to Meitner for help
checks.note: Letter of 19 December 1938 (Wikipedia); Grokipedia says letters of 19 and 22 December.

checks.claim: Meitner was Hahn's research partner of 'nearly thirty years'
checks.note: The partnership began in late 1907 and ended when she left on 13 July 1938, so about thirty and a half years: 'nearly thirty' undershoots. Grokipedia's Meitner page says both 'over three decades' and 'nearly 30 years'; Wikipedia notes they had not worked together for some years before 1934. Safe fix: 'his research partner of some thirty years'.

checks.claim: Meitner had fled Nazi Germany that summer
checks.note: Fled on 13-14 July 1938 to the Netherlands, then Stockholm; Austrian citizenship lost after the Anschluss.

checks.claim: At Christmas in Sweden she and her nephew Otto Frisch worked out what the barium meant
checks.note: Christmas 1938 at Kungälv; Frisch was her nephew.

checks.claim: Key: the nucleus had split into two smaller nuclei
checks.note: Liquid-drop picture; two fragments lighter by about a fifth of a proton mass, about 200 MeV.

checks.claim: Wrong: a neutron had chipped a small piece off the nucleus
checks.note: Truly wrong: barium (56) is far from uranium (92); chipping would leave an element near uranium.

checks.claim: Wrong: neutrons had built it up into a heavier element
checks.note: Truly wrong for the barium: this was Fermi's and the Berlin team's earlier transuranium reading, which the barium overturned.

checks.claim: Wrong: the barium had been mixed in from the start
checks.note: Truly wrong: the barium was radioactive and appeared only after neutron bombardment (their 'radium' activities proved to be barium).

checks.claim: Context: barium has 56 protons, little more than half of uranium's 92
checks.note: Ba Z=56 (Grokipedia Barium), U Z=92. 56/92 = 0.61; 'little more than half' is a fair plain-words gloss.

checks.claim: Context: Fermi and the Berlin team had earlier read such products as elements heavier than uranium
checks.note: Fermi 'tentatively concluded' elements 93 and 94; Berlin concluded 'they were indeed transuranium elements'.

checks.claim: Context: Hahn and Strassmann reported the barium but, as chemists, held back from explaining it
checks.note: True in substance ('we cannot yet bring ourselves to take this step'). Small nuance: the paper says that AS CHEMISTS they must name barium, and as 'nuclear chemists' they hesitate. Optional: 'reported the barium but held back from explaining it, leaving that to physicists'.

checks.claim: Context: Frisch named the split fission, after the way a living cell divides
checks.note: Frisch asked William A. Arnold what biologists call cell division; Arnold said fission.

checks.claim: Context: Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Meitner was left out
checks.note: Announced 15 November 1945 (deferred a year), presented December 1945; the context names the prize year only, which is correct.

checks.claim: A helium nucleus has less mass than two free protons and two free neutrons, and every nucleus of more than one particle shows the shortfall
checks.note: Measured nuclear masses 'are always less than the sum of the masses of protons and neutrons that form them'.

checks.claim: Physicists call it the mass defect
Key: some of their mass left as energy when they joined
checks.note: The missing mass 'represents the energy that was released when the nucleus was formed'.

checks.claim: Wrong: stored inside as heat; packed tightly take less room; gravity pulls more weakly
checks.note: All truly wrong: energy kept inside would keep the mass; volume and gravity do not change rest mass.

checks.claim: Context: Einstein's E = mc^2; mass and energy can turn into each other
checks.note: Standard school wording. Grokipedia warns against 'mass is destroyed'; the context's next sentence ('energy leaves and carries that sliver of mass away') gives the exact picture, so it stays true.

checks.claim: Context: one gram is worth about 90 trillion joules
checks.note: About 9 x 10^13 J per gram.

checks.claim: Context: chemical reactions shift mass by about a billionth, too little to weigh, so chemists find mass conserved
checks.note: 'on the order of 10^-9 or less', 'far below measurable thresholds'.

checks.claim: Frisch tested the splitting idea in Copenhagen in January 1939
checks.note: The experiment was done on 13 January 1939; letter in Nature 143 (1939).

checks.claim: Uranium-lined counting chamber, neutron source beside it, counter set to record only pulses far bigger than uranium's alpha particles
checks.note: Uranium-lined ionization chamber; thyratron biased to count pulses of at least 5 x 10^5 ion pairs; radium-beryllium source 1 cm from the lining; alpha pulses 'much smaller'.

checks.claim: Key: big pulses with the source taken away would have counted most against the idea
checks.note: Sound reasoning; the check runs of several hours without the source recorded no pulses.

checks.claim: Wrong: no big pulses with the uranium lining removed
checks.note: What he saw; supports the idea.

checks.claim: Wrong: twice as many pulses with paraffin round the source
checks.note: What he saw (a factor of two); supports the idea, since slow neutrons split uranium more readily.

checks.claim: Wrong: fewer pulses with a weaker source
checks.note: What he saw: the count varied linearly with source strength; supports the idea.

checks.claim: Context: Frisch called his pulses conclusive evidence of uranium nuclei breaking into pieces of comparable size
checks.note: Faithful paraphrase (not in quotation marks) of 'conclusive physical evidence for the breaking up of uranium nuclei into parts of comparable size'.

checks.claim: Key: new neutrons thrown out by each split carry the chain reaction
checks.note: 'released neutrons trigger further splits'.

checks.claim: Wrong: heat bursting the next nucleus
checks.note: Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: the two flying pieces of each split
checks.note: Truly wrong: the charged fragments slow in the fuel and give up their energy as heat.

checks.claim: Wrong: radiation from each split, weakening the next
checks.note: Truly wrong as worded. Neutrons are themselves a kind of radiation, but 'weakening the next' is no mechanism, and the key is plainly the best answer.

checks.claim: Context: U-235 splits when it captures a neutron; each split throws out two or three neutrons
checks.note: Average 2.43 prompt neutrons per fission. (A minority of captures make U-236 without splitting; a fine 9th-grade simplification.)

checks.claim: Context: the two pieces carry most of the energy as speed, which becomes heat
checks.note: About 85% of the ~200 MeV is fragment kinetic energy (about 170 MeV).

checks.claim: Context: a fuel pellet about a centimetre across gives about as much energy as a ton of coal
checks.note: NEI and Utah's energy office give about one ton of coal per pellet; whatisnuclear.com calculates about 1.3 t. Pellets are about 1 cm (fingertip size).

checks.claim: Context: a split frees millions of times more energy than a chemical reaction
checks.note: 'millions of times that of chemical reactions'.

checks.claim: Safety lane
checks.note: 'A lump of such uranium' is generic; no enrichment level, critical mass or weapon detail.

checks.claim: Stem: fission heats water into steam, which spins a turbine driving a generator
Stem: control rods of boron or cadmium slide in and out; all the way in they stop the chain reaction
checks.note: Materials 'such as boron carbide, cadmium, hafnium'; a scram inserts the rods 'to halt the reaction'.

checks.claim: Key: they soak up neutrons before those split more nuclei
checks.note: 'a neutron-absorbing rod'; 'deeper insertion absorbs more neutrons to decrease power output'.

checks.claim: Wrong: they slow the neutrons down so fewer nuclei split
checks.note: Truly wrong: slowing is the moderator's job, and slow neutrons split U-235 more readily.

checks.claim: Wrong: they cool the uranium; they bounce neutrons back out
checks.note: Truly wrong: rods absorb; cooling is the coolant's job and bouncing neutrons back is a reflector's.

checks.claim: Context: the moderator, usually the water round the fuel, slows neutrons, and slow neutrons split U-235 more readily
checks.note: 'Light water serves as the predominant neutron moderator'; U-235 has 'much higher absorption cross-sections for thermal neutrons'.

checks.claim: Context: 'the same water carries the heat away as steam'
checks.note: False for most reactors. In a pressurized water reactor (more than 65% of US reactors, and most worldwide) the water round the fuel is kept under pressure so it does not boil; it heats a separate loop of water, and that water becomes the steam. Only boiling water reactors turn the core water itself to steam. Fix: '...; the same water carries the heat away to make the steam.'

checks.claim: Fusion joins light nuclei into heavier ones; fusion machines try to join deuterium and tritium (heavy hydrogen) into helium
checks.note: D + T gives helium-4 + a neutron. Most fusion machines (tokamaks, NIF) use D-T; a few private ventures try other fuels, which is fine at this level.

checks.claim: The fuel must be heated to 100 million degrees Celsius or more, into a plasma of bare nuclei and loose electrons
checks.note: Best D-T temperature 'between 100 and 200 million Kelvin'; plasma is 'ionized gas'.

checks.claim: Key: only fast nuclei get close despite pushing each other away
checks.note: 'electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei' must be overcome before the short-range strong force takes over (tunnelling helps; fine to omit at grade 9).

checks.claim: Wrong: melt to flow together; break into loose protons first; burn with oxygen
checks.note: All truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: the helium and neutron have a little less mass than the fuel; the missing mass leaves as energy; nothing burns
checks.note: 17.6 MeV from the mass defect.

checks.claim: Context: plasma held by magnetic fields (tokamak) or fuel pellets crushed with lasers
checks.note: Magnetic and inertial confinement. (At NIF the lasers heat a gold can whose X-rays crush the pellet; 'crush with lasers' is fair shorthand.)

checks.claim: NIF in California, 192 lasers, frozen deuterium-tritium pellet, 5 December 2022
checks.note: Correct. Strictly, the beams go into a tiny gold cylinder (hohlraum) holding the pellet, not onto the pellet itself; 'aimed at a pellet' is acceptable shorthand in the stem if the context is fixed (below).

checks.claim: The team announced that for the first time a shot had reached ignition
checks.note: LLNL: 'the first controlled fusion experiment in history to reach this milestone'. (An August 2021 shot was later said to meet the Lawson criterion, but the stem reports the December 2022 announcement, and its definition is the one the key uses.)

checks.claim: Key: the pellet gave out more energy than the lasers put in
checks.note: 'scientific energy breakeven, meaning it produced more energy from fusion than the laser energy used to drive it': 3.15 MJ out against 2.05 MJ delivered to the target.

checks.claim: Wrong: the laboratory made more energy than it drew from the grid
checks.note: Truly wrong: the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid.

checks.claim: Wrong: sent out as electricity to homes; went on fusing for hours
checks.note: Truly wrong: no electricity was made, and the burn lasts a split second.

checks.claim: Context: '2.05 megajoules of laser light that reached the pellet'
checks.note: The laser light did not reach the pellet. It 'reached the small cylindrical chamber known as a hohlraum, which converts the UV to x rays', and the capsule took in only about 250 kJ. LLNL says the 2.05 MJ was delivered 'to the target' (the gold can with the pellet inside). Fix: 'against the 2.05 megajoules of laser light fired into the tiny gold can that held the pellet'.

checks.claim: Context: the first time any fusion experiment got more energy out of its fuel than its lasers put in
Context: the lasers drew about 300 megajoules from the grid for the split-second shot
checks.note: 'each laser shot requires about 300 MJ of energy from the grid' (Scientific American gives 322 MJ).

checks.claim: Context: no fusion machine yet makes more electricity than it uses
checks.note: True as of November 2026: 'no device yet producing more electricity than consumed'. Realta's June 2026 direct-conversion demo was stated by its makers not to be net electricity. A changing fact; recheck before each release.

checks.claim: Context: later shots have given out more than 8 megajoules
checks.note: 8.6 MJ on 7 April 2025 (LLNL annual report). 'More than 8' survives future records.

checks.claim: Nuclear plants make about a tenth of the world's electricity
checks.note: 8.9% in 2025 (Ember); 'about 9%' (Grokipedia Nuclear power). The share is drifting down slowly; 'about a tenth' holds for now.

checks.claim: A plant runs day and night whatever the weather
checks.note: US plants at full power more than 92% of the time. (Heat waves occasionally force cutbacks; fine as plain words against wind and solar.)

checks.claim: Over its life it gives off about as little CO2 per unit of electricity as a wind farm
checks.note: IPCC 2014 medians: nuclear 12, onshore wind 11, offshore wind 12 g CO2eq/kWh; UNECE: nuclear 5.1, wind 12-14.

checks.claim: Every year or two part of its fuel is used up and comes out
checks.note: Refuelling 'typically every 1.5 or 2 years'.

checks.claim: Key: used fuel stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years
checks.note: 'stays a radiation hazard for extended periods of time'; a repository must keep it from people 'for thousands of years'.

checks.claim: Wrong: it is a liquid that leaks from tanks
checks.note: Truly wrong: 'a solid when it goes into the reactor and a solid when it comes out'.

checks.claim: Wrong: it piles up by the millions of tonnes every year
checks.note: Truly wrong: the US makes about 2,000 t a year; a 1,000 MWe reactor discharges 20-30 t (Grokipedia Nuclear power).

checks.claim: Wrong: it leaks radiation whenever it is moved by road or rail
checks.note: Wrong as meant (and it is a transport claim, not a storage one). Note that a loaded cask always gives off a little radiation through its walls, within legal limits; to make the choice airtight, consider 'It spills out of its casks whenever it is moved by road or by rail'.

checks.claim: Context: solid ceramic pellets in metal rods; cooled for years in pools that carry off heat and block radiation; then sealed casks of steel and concrete
checks.note: Pools are used 'to cool it and provide shielding from its radioactivity' (Wikipedia Spent nuclear fuel).

checks.claim: Context: all US used fuel since the 1950s would fit on one football field less than 10 yards deep
Context: 'thousands of cask shipments have crossed the country with no release of radiation'
checks.note: Minor wording. DOE says more than 2,500 shipments went 'without any radiological releases', meaning no radioactive material escaped. A loaded transport cask always gives off some radiation through its walls (US rules cap it at about 10 millirem an hour two metres away: https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML0100/ML010050022.pdf), so 'no release of radiation' teaches that casks let none out. Fix: 'thousands of cask shipments have crossed the country without any radioactive material escaping.'

checks.claim: Context: it must be kept away from people for thousands of years, and Finland has built the world's first deep underground store
checks.note: Onkalo is built; Finland granted its operating licence on 22 October 2026, with disposal to begin after final commissioning and inspection. 'Has built' is right; do not change it to 'operates' until disposal begins.

unit_notes: Safety lane clean: no enrichment level, critical mass or weapon detail in any stem, choice or context (Q6's 'a lump of such uranium' is generic; NIF's weapons mission is not mentioned). Every key and every wrong choice holds up; the errors are context wording only: Q1 (range is not why electrons escape the strong force), Q7 (in most reactors the core water does not itself become the steam), Q9 (the laser light hit the gold hohlraum, not the pellet), Q10 ('no release of radiation' should be no radioactive material escaping). Q3 is uncertain on 'nearly thirty years' (late 1907 to July 1938 is just over thirty). Changing facts to recheck: fusion net electricity (Q9), the 8.6 MJ NIF record (Q9 says 'more than 8', safe), nuclear's world share (8.9% in 2025), Onkalo's start of disposal (Q10 says 'has built', safe). Note for facts.md: F27 quotes Grokipedia calling Onkalo 'operational'; as of November 2026 it is licensed (22 October 2026) but not yet disposing of fuel.
